thread.title: Apple's Universe Should Brace for a Recession

title: Apple's Universe Should Brace for a Recession

organizations.name: heather seidel/the wall street journal lumentum

text:
Apple’s Universe Should Brace for a Recession By Nov. 12, 2018 3:21 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photography by Stephanie Keith/Getty Images Text size
Lumentum ’s largest customer is Apple (ticker: AAPL), accounting for almost one-third of its sales. Monday morning, the supplier cut its guidance for revenue by about 17%, raising concern about demand for Apple goods and sending its own stock down nearly 30%.
Companies in Apple’s supply chain are feeling the pain. The 54 Apple suppliers Barron’s tracks were down about 4%, on average, by early afternoon.
The shock wave from the announcement continues to ripple outward. For instance, Lumentum’s (LITE) own suppliers—companies like Veeco Instruments (VECO) and Fabrinet (FN)—fell about 5%. Apple shares were down about 5% as well. Apple reached a market value of $1 trillion on Thursday, propelled by the sustained success of the iPhone. WSJ's Spencer Jakab takes a look at how Apple got here. Photo illustration: Heather Seidel/The Wall Street Journal
Lumentum’s troubles perfectly illustrate the perils of a company relying too heavily on a few customers, but the news also highlights a key reality for the Apple universe.
The iPhone has matured. It’s 11 years old and it isn’t growing like it used to, as the chart below shows. Updating it will be difficult from now on, given that Apple management will no longer disclose iPhone sales volumes on their quarterly conference calls.
Analysts seem to be tacitly endorsing the idea that iPhone sales will now be more cyclical. JPMorgan Chase analyst Samik Chatterjee wrote to clients Monday suggesting that investors should, “look past cyclical volumes” and focus instead on secular growth in the services business at Apple.
Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
In the past, the iPhone itself was a secular growth engine. Growth in services is well and good for Apple stock, but it isn't a driver for growth at the tech giant’s suppliers.
It also doesn’t appear that tech investors were ready for slower iPhone growth. The stock prices of Apple suppliers have tracked iPhone shipments over time, but they got ahead of growth in unit sales last November, perhaps because of optimism about the coming product cycle.
Now that looks like a miscalculation. So what lessons do supply-chain investors need to learn to prosper under the lower-growth paradigm?
First and foremost, they must realize that growth inflections are rocky. The performance of the stocks already tells us that.
And stories about excessive inventories will take longer to resolve themselves than in the past. Growth in unit sales of iPhones can’t save the day when demand for a specific model may have been misjudged. It’s likely the iPhone production cuts implied by Lumentum’s news are going to weigh on supply-chain sentiment for at least the next two quarters.
Apple supply-chain investors are also going to have to learn what it’s like investing through a recession. That’s right, a recession. The last time the economy experienced an actual recession, from 2007 through 2009, Apple was shipping about 20 million iPhones annually. The company ships over 217 million units a year now—more than 10-fold growth without experiencing an economic downturn.
The overall economy may keep powering ahead, but given the number of unsold iPhones out there, Apple won’t have to produce as many to meet flattening demand. That Apple universe will have to live through a downturn.
That’s what happens in the auto industry when dealers’ inventories get too high. The sales problem is compounded by the inventory problem.
When demand for cars—another pillar of the global economy—slows, light vehicle unit sales drop 10%-20%. The stocks can fall roughly double that amount as profit estimates are cut and price/earnings multiples contract.
Of course, cars are $20,000 credit-financed purchases, and iPhones cost about $1,000, so the depth of an iPhone-recession wouldn’t likely be that severe. There is also an argument that a smartphone isn’t a discretionary item, like a car, and is more like a consumer staple in today’s world.
Given all of this cyclical “learning,” have suppliers fallen far enough? After all, the production problems have already taken a big toll on the group. For example, capital-equipment supplier Cognex (CGNX) is down 23% since the start of October and server maker Super Micro Computer (SMCI) is down more than 40%. Newsletter Sign-up
Does that represent good value or a value trap? That’s another question cyclical investors often ask that tech investors will need to learn.
Cyclical stocks don’t always come back until the underlying top-line outlook improves. That means iPhone production may have to rise before the suppliers’ stocks come back, regardless of valuations.
More diversified suppliers like Intel (INTC) and Qualcomm (QCOM) will be less dependent on news about Apple. Those stocks’ multiples have contracted by 10% to 20% since the beginning of October. They are a safer way to test the value versus value-trap paradigm in 2019.
